title: The stolen pears (Confessions 2)
hook: Augustine remembers stealing pears as a boy, not from hunger, just to do wrong

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerome's Bible, the Vulgate. Your line was ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ.
screen: `IGNORANCE OF SCRIPTURE IS IGNORANCE OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: It's late at night, and a gang of boys has stayed out in the streets longer than they should. Near a vineyard stands a pear tree, loaded with fruit. The pears aren't much to look at, and not much to taste. The boys shake the tree anyway and carry off armfuls. They eat a few. The rest they throw to the pigs. One of those boys grew up to be Augustine, and years later, writing his Confessions, he couldn't let that night go. He kept asking one question about it.

The Confessions is a long prayer: Augustine tells his life to God, on the page. And of everything he could linger on, he stops at a pear tree. He wasn't hungry, he says. He had better pears at home. He didn't want the fruit. He wanted the stealing. He loved the wrong itself. That honesty is the strange gift of this chapter. It's easy to explain small wrongs away: I was tired, I was provoked, everybody does it. Augustine refuses the excuse. He keeps looking for the reason, and the first answer is ugly: he did it because it wasn't allowed. Then he finds a second. He would not have done it alone. It was the company: the laughing, the daring, not wanting to be the one who held back. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. So the theft wasn't only about pears. It was about belonging. Paul had put words to this tangle in his letter to the Romans: "for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I." Some readers connect the chapter with Augustine's later teaching on the bent of the human will and on original sin. Others read it more simply, as a man telling the truth about a night he'd rather forget. Either way, he doesn't stop at the guilt. The whole book is spoken to the God he believes forgave him. Naming the wrong is the first step. Finding the reason is the second.

Let one small wrong from long ago come to mind, nothing heavy: something taken, a lie told, a cruelty you joined in. Don't defend it, and don't punish yourself with it; just ask Augustine's question: was it the thing itself, the doing, or the people watching? If you pray, tell God the reason you find; if you don't, simply let yourself know it.
Augustine. His boyhood theft of pears, done not from hunger, but for the wrong itself, and for the company.
Your line: know why you do it. The pears were never really about pears. That's today.

howItsDone: Augustine's Confessions is read by Christians of different churches as a model of honest self-examination; some use the practice of examining the day, or the examination of conscience before confession, in the same spirit.

fork.reveal: he wasn't hungry and didn't want the fruit. he found two reasons: the wrong itself, and the friends who were with him.

chat.says: Why would a saint write a whole chapter about stealing pears as a kid?
options: He wasn't hungry; he wanted the stealing and the company, and he dug for why.
He was starving as a boy, and wanted readers to see how poor his family was.
He wanted to show that small childhood wrongs aren't worth thinking about.
chat.meaning: Augustine had better pears at home. He loved the wrong itself and the company, and he refused the easy excuse to find the real reason.
